references.text: Some asked whether Christ could come from Galilee, pointing to the Scriptures that said the Messiah would come from Bethlehem. This skepticism about Jesus' origin recalls Nathanael's doubt that anything good could come from Nazareth ([ref:Joh 7:41-42|John 7:41-42]).
The Pharisees rejected the idea that any prophet could come from Galilee, reflecting the same prejudice against Nazareth and Galilee that Nathanael expressed ([ref:Joh 7:52|John 7:52]).

Philip had just told Nathanael that they had found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about—Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael's question in verse 46 is a direct response to this ([ref:Joh 1:45|John 1:45]).
Despite his initial skepticism, Nathanael recognized Jesus as the Son of God and King of Israel after meeting him—he followed Philip's invitation "Come and see" ([ref:Joh 1:47-49|John 1:47-49]).
Matthew notes that Jesus was to be called a Nazarene according to the prophets, linking to the low expectations associated with Nazareth that Nathanael expressed ([ref:Matt 2:23|Matthew 2:23]).

The prophecy about the suffering servant who grows up "like a tender shoot from dry ground", despised and unimpressive, reflects the idea that something good and great can come from what seems insignificant—as Nazareth was viewed ([ref:Jes 53:2-3|Isaiah 53:2-3]).
The Samaritan woman's invitation "Come and see" recalls Philip's words to Nathanael, where personal experience with Jesus overcomes skepticism ([ref:Joh 4:29|John 4:29]).

The prophecy about a shoot from the stump of Jesse uses the Hebrew word "netser" (shoot), which linguistically connects to Nazareth (Natseret). From something seemingly insignificant, the Messiah still emerges ([ref:Jes 11:1|Isaiah 11:1]).
The Jews were skeptical about Jesus because they knew his earthly parents and origin—the same kind of prejudice against Jesus' background that Nathanael showed ([ref:Joh 6:42|John 6:42]).
